Title: Tournament Report: Anarch Revolt Los Angeles

Messages.Author: Third Planet
Messages.Body:
This is being posted from my work e-mail address. Hi folks
- We had a bang up time here last Saturday, as 14 Meths came
together to duel in a marathon of V:TES. The drafting began
at 11:30 am, and the final round ended at 10:30 pm.

Without further ado, here are the results:

The standings after 3 rounds were as follows:

Mike Courtois 9.5 VP, 174 TP, 60 Blood
Paul Johnson 7.5 VP, 180 TP, 77 Bood
Robyn Merrill 4.5 VP, 144 TP, 13 Blood
Steve Bucy 4 VP, 124 TP, 24 Blood

Andre Caceras 0 VP, 54 TP, 0 Blood
Dennis Lien 0 VP, 28 TP, 0 Blood

Every round was a drag-out slugfest, as people were trying
their best to make do with what cards they drafted. The
final seating order was Wade, Paul, Steve, Robyn, Mike (I
don't remember who ended up going first). Mike Courtois had
dominated in the early rounds with lots of stealth, and as
such was the target when it came time for the finals.
Although at times it seemed like he was fighting four other
methuselahs, he still managed to gain a VP by pounding heck
out of poor Wade and then Ancilla Empowerment-ing both he
and Wade out at the same time. As always, the psychological
warfare was at a fever pitch, with psychmaster Steve Bucy
("Oh man, I can't believe how bad my crypt draw is") finally
coming out on top. I have posted his deck below, mostly to
show what kind of kitchen sink decks end up working in a
draft tournament. The VP distribution in the final round
was as follows, in order of finish:
Steve Bucy 2 VP, Mike Courtois 1VP, Robyn Merrill 1VP, Paul
Johnson 0VP, Wade von Grawbadger 0VP.

A few items of note:

Even in this limited environment, Life Boon reared its ugly
head four times, and probably prevented Wade from a much
higher seating in the finals. Does it need to be banned? A
question for those smarter than I, but I feel that a *one*
card play that really can only be trumped by another card
(sudden reversal) should not have so much influence.

We did straight Rochester Draft. Each pack took about 20
minutes to draft, and that was with folks going at a good
clip. We had 2 drafting pods of 7 players apiece. Many of
the participants commented that the draft process takes too
long. I would have to agree. I think that perhaps the
Elder Draft that Carl Philsatch is suggesting would make for
a better, and perhaps quicker draft. Other comments were
that 5 packs were not enough, maybe drop 1-3 sealed packs in
as well, so that there was a little more deck-building
skills involved. I am not sure I agree. If you get up in
the 120-150 card range, decks can start to get pretty tuned
(especially with a deck of 40 cards), and the "level playing
field" changes. And as Paul Johnson (no relation to LSJ)
pointed out, the draft is actually part of the deck-building
process.

They are *usable* but I sincerly doubt that they work well für VTES.
Rochester and Booster were designed for Magic. The problem is that
Magic and VTES are quite different, in regards to crypt/library and
lands in Magic.
Oh yes, you definitely can draft one booster after the other (with both
Rochester and Booster style), but it creates some awkward situations.
You might (and will) end up with some boosters which don't correspond
at all with the cards you drafted so far. E.g. the second booster to
go, and you already have decided to go for Gangrel with pro. You have 4
Gangrel, and a couple of pro cards. But bad luck: you don't get to draw
anymore Gangrels. You end up with a load of pro cards, but no Gangrels
to use them! Ok, you could adapt your needs with every booster, but is
that a desireable situation?
If you draft all vampires in one go at the beginning, you know exactly
what you have in terms of skills, and know what to go for, and what
substitutes you could draft.
Now, don't get me wrong, I know that you can't possible expect to have
a higly focussed deck, but when you draft all vamps before the library,
you can decide *better* on a strategy!
And, it's easy to handle, we have tried it out many times, and at the
EC 59 players were drafting with this system, so experience and
reliable data (if we can agree upon that it is somewhat reliable) is at
hand.

You end up with "a load" of pro cards only if you are not paying attention
to the fact that you haven't got any vampires to use them. Smart drafting
will avoid this problem.

> to use them! Ok, you could adapt your needs with every booster, but is
> that a desireable situation?

Yes.
That is inherent in the nature of draft.
There are no guarantees that you will get the cards you need to make
a "tuned" deck.

How does the Elder Draft ensure that a player will be able to draft
the cards he wants?

If your group/area/tourney scene has trouble/takes issue with this
sort of thing (not being able to draft an appropriate crypt), then you
are welcome to implement [DCI 62], e.g., making all vampires freely
available to your players who are then free to focus on drafting their
libraries. (or vice-versa :-).

> If you draft all vampires in one go at the beginning, you know exactly
> what you have in terms of skills, and know what to go for, and what
> substitutes you could draft.

But what if you draft all Gangrels only to discover that the boosters
don't correspond to your choice (i.e., they are very light on PRO and
ANI and FOR)?

> Now, don't get me wrong, I know that you can't possible expect to have
> a higly focussed deck, but when you draft all vamps before the library,
> you can decide *better* on a strategy!

Or, if you draft all your library first, you can decide on a better
strategy for drafting vampires.

Or you can mix the two, developing your strategy as you see what cards
you are able to draft (which refines your draft strategy, and so on).

Seriously - that's what happens. Give it a try.

> And, it's easy to handle, we have tried it out many times, and at the
> EC 59 players were drafting with this system, so experience and
> reliable data (if we can agree upon that it is somewhat reliable) is at
> hand.

Data for the current system is also on hand. At least for those who have
tried the system.

And the current system doesn't suffer from the drawback that the Elder Draft
has - namely of opening more than one pack per player at a time (something
the DCI frowns on).

We've been over all these points already, if you recall.

deck. However things quickly changed as everyone drafted the dominate minion
cards and most of the Ventrue. I then switched to Gangrel/Ventrue. At one
point there were no vamps I could use so I picked up some Malks for the
obfiscate. As the draft went on, and grabbed what I could get, it became
more of a aggravated combat deck with lots of defense. After the draft I
noticed many huge weeknesses in the deck. 1) No intercept. I just wasn't
able to draft any, not even a Cats Guidance. Only Andreas, if I got him in
my crypt could help. 2) Little vote power. 3) No rush. Very bad for a
mostly combat deck. 4) lack of stealth. Only if I got one of three vamps
with Obfiscate or two with superior protean would I have ready stealth. In
the two rounds I did well, I got out a vamp with obfiscate and superior
protean...

I was left wondering what, if anything this deck would do. It appeared to
have almost no offense, no active defense, and almost no political power.

My strategy was simple... look as pathetic as the deck really was.
Relentlessly harrass my prey with one point bleeds in the hope they would
block and I could get them in combat. If I got them down low I would
hopefully have a threats and some stealth to give them a good hit. On
defense: Leave blockers untapped and pray my preditor didn't have any
stealth or votes...

Folks (LSJ & Carl):

At US GenCon (a WotC event) the last several years they have been using
a "Michigan Draft" which sounds just like the Elder Draft. That is,
everyone opens their packs and places the vampires into one pile and
the library into another. Each of the two piles is thoroughly shuffled
(no small feat) and then the vampire pile is drafted in Rochester
style. After that, the library pile is drafted.

From my experience, this is an excellent method of drafting for the
reasons Carl mentions. In particular, you are able to know who your
vampires first are so you can draft an appropriate library. This is
most critical if you have/like/use vampires with lesser-frequency
disciplines, like Protean or Thaumaturgy.

The reason that Booster and Rochester work so well in Magic is that
a drafter gets the land that she needs (in any quantity and
distribution) *after* she drafts a library. What if there were more
types of lands (say, 10 basic instead of just 5) and these players had
to draft land at the same time as their library? It just wouldn't work
out as well, would it?

Yours,

On Wed, 26 Jan 2000 carlos_...@my-deja.com wrote:
> > But going in with narrow
> > ideas about exactly what you want to play is always difficult,
> especially
> > in a game with as many variations of disciplines as Jyhad.
>
> What do you consider narrow ideas? A bleed concept? A clan concept? A
> discipline-concept?

A clan or very narrow discipline concept, essentially (which should throw
earlier comments into greater clarity).

Going in thinking "I will play the best Gangrel deck I can get out of
this" is, perhaps, a little foolish, if you follow through with the idea.
Ideas such as "combat deck" or "bleed and vote" seem fine, to me, but
going in with something like "Gangrel protean" deck or "Giovanni" deck,
where the options are *so* much narrower seems like making a noose for
yourself. People will see things like the Protean cards and, since they
may have a few vampires capable of using them, they won't be seriously
disadvantaged with them *and* they get to screw you badly, as previously
discussed.

> And we seem to agree that Jyhad is a very complex game, with many
> disciplines and clans, quite different to Magic's 5 colours (or are
> there new colours in the new sets? :) )

Purple, anyone? ;)
